content: Baryte, also known as barium sulfate (BaSO4), is a mineral primarily composed of barium sulfate. It is typically white or colorless and serves as the principal source of barium. The American spelling of the mineral is barite, while baryte is the older, unofficial spelling. The mineral is also referred to as heavy spar or tiff. A specific radiating form of baryte, sometimes called Bologna Stone, gained historical attention among alchemists in the 1600s due to its phosphorescent properties, which were first observed in specimens discovered near Bologna by Vincenzo Cascariolo. The crystal structure of baryte is orthorhombic. It is commonly found in lead-zinc veins within limestones, in deposits formed by hot springs, and in association with hematite ore. Baryte is frequently found alongside other minerals such as anglesite and celestine. The name baryte is derived from the Greek word βαρύς, meaning heavy, reflecting its high specific gravity. In commercial contexts, the mineral is sometimes referred to as barytes. When the International Mineralogical Association was established in 1959, the American spelling barite was adopted as the official term, but this decision was reversed in 1978. The term primary baryte refers to the initial marketable product, which includes crude baryte (directly mined material) and products obtained through basic beneficiation processes such as washing, jigging, heavy media separation, tabling, flotation, and magnetic separation. Most crude baryte requires further refinement to meet minimum standards of purity or density. When used as an aggregate in heavy cement, baryte is crushed and screened to achieve a uniform particle size. For other applications, baryte is typically ground into a fine, uniform powder. Approximately 77% of the global baryte supply is utilized as a weighting agent in drilling fluids for oil and gas exploration. Other applications include its use in high-value industries such as automotive manufacturing, electronics, television screens, rubber, glass ceramics, and paint production. Baryte is also employed in radiation shielding and medical applications, such as barium meals used in diagnostic imaging. The mineral is available in various forms, and its price depends on the degree of processing. Applications requiring baryte as a filler demand higher prices due to the intensive physical processing involved, such as grinding and micronizing. Additional premiums are applied for qualities like whiteness, brightness, and color. Baryte is also used in the production of paints and paper. Despite containing the heavy metal barium, baryte is not considered toxic by most regulatory authorities due to its extreme insolubility, which minimizes its bioavailability and environmental impact.
